list 2 of 3 Yemen’s Taiz residents fear food and fuel crisis amid fighting
list 3 of 3 More than 200,000 displaced as fighting escalates in Yemen, UN says
It said emergency care, surgery, intensive care, dialysis and neonatal services could be forced to stop if the situation continued, putting patients, injured people, pregnant women and newborns “at immediate risk”.
Fuel shortages also threaten electricity generators, ambulances and the cold chains that keep medicines and vaccines usable, which could cause “severe complications and preventable deaths”, the ministry said.
It demanded the siege be lifted immediately, and supply routes reopened, with safe passage for patients, ambulances, health workers and aid.
It called on the United Nations and humanitarian organisations to “deliver medicines, intravenous fluids, medical supplies, oxygen and fuel” to the city’s health facilities.
“Every delay increases the risk of service interruption and loss of life,” the ministry said.
The Houthis, an armed group backed by Iran and also known as Ansar Allah, seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, by force in 2014 and later imposed their own government. They control the country’s north and northeast.
Taiz endured a devastating Houthi siege between 2015 and 2016, when Yemeni government forces were confined to an enclave in the city centre.
The siege was broken in 2016, though the Houthis kept a partial blockade through other access points. In 2024, they agreed to reopen a route from the east, but it has been closed after fighting resumed.
The Houthis launched an offensive along the Red Sea coast of the Taiz governorate in September, capturing the port city of Mocha, and by October 4 had taken the town of At Turbah, cutting the last main road between Taiz city and other government-held areas.
Yemeni government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, began a counteroffensive in early October.
Nabil Jamil, director-general of the Yemeni government’s planning and development office in the Taiz governorate, told Al Jazeera the current siege is “more comprehensive and its impact more severe than in 2015”.
He said about 2.8 million people live in government-held areas of the governorate, along with 200,000 who have recently been displaced.
Fuel has become scarce, and on the black market, the price of a 20-litre (5.2-gallon) container of petrol has risen from 30,000 Yemeni riyals ($19) to 90,000 ($58).
“We are still waiting for a response or intervention on the ground,” Jamil said.
The UN refugee agency and the World Health Organization have warned that the fighting is putting Yemen’s fragile health system in peril.
“Civilians must never be turned into a means of exerting pressure in any conflict,” said Nabil Sharyan, a lawyer and head of the Justice for Rights and Development Organization.

items.title: Nobel peace laureate says US sanctions on ICC 'unacceptable'
items.summary: Navi Pillay says the Trump administrations' sweeping penalties on the international tribunal were "unheard of".
items.content:
Image caption, The South African former ICC judge was awarded the prize on Friday
Navi Pillay, the winner of this year's Nobel Peace Prize, has called US sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) "unheard of" and "unacceptable".
The South African former ICC judge was awarded the prize on Friday "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said.
US President Donald Trump expressed his disatisfaction with the pick and hours later the US unveiled sweeping sanctions in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it described as a "rogue" institution.
The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.
Pillay, speaking via video link during an event at the Nobel Peace Center in Oslo on Saturday, said: "There is so much tension and anxiety over the continued existence of international courts, mainly the International Criminal Court in The Hague.
"Most importantly, sanctions have been announced by one country against the judges, just for the judicial orders they issue. This is unheard of, unacceptable."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier said the sanctions - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.
The US has already sanctioned 17 ICC judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to inhibit its ability to operate financially.
However, the US has provided a six-month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns.
The Trump administration claims that the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty.
It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar".
The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in saying they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions.
Figure caption, Watch: Who is Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay?
Pillay, 85, also served as UN rights chief, taking part in high-profile work considering allegations of human rights violations, including in Rwanda, Myanmar and Gaza.
Her early work included defending anti-apartheid activists in South Africa, and on Friday she became the country's fifth Peace Prize winner - following in the footsteps of Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu.
"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked after receiving the prize, a reference to last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition figure MarÃ­a Corina Machado, deciding to gift her prize to the US president.
Trump called the announcement of Pillay as 2026's winner "disgraceful and embarassing", and an "indelible stain on the country of Norway".
He has long indicated he thought he should have been awarded the prestigious prize, and was nominated by several allies for it last year.

Ship captains and crews transiting the Strait of Hormuz make so much danger pay that they’re ‘almost being viewed as mercenaries’
Iran's medium-sized oil tankers continue to wait off the coast of Bandar Abbas at the Strait of Hormuz in Hormozgan Province, Iran on September 9, 2026. Fatemeh Bahrami/Anadolu via Getty Images
The high-risk, high-reward business of moving oil through the Strait of Hormuz has gotten riskier and more rewarding.
Despite steady attacks from Iran, oil tankers and other commercial vessels have continued flowing through the narrow waterway. With protection from the U.S. military and help from pipelines bypassing the strait, Persian Gulf oil flows returned to prewar levels .
But seeking to reassert its leverage over the global oil chokepoint, Iran has stepped up drone and missile strikes on ships recently, including those outside the immediate vicinity of Hormuz.
While traffic has dipped in response, ships continue to cross, with many making shuttle runs in and out of the Gulf to unload oil cargoes via ship-to-ship transfers. Then other vessels deliver the barrels to customers.
For those onboard the ships willing to tolerate the risks in the Gulf, a hefty payday awaits. Tanker captains can earn $100,000 a month for transiting the strait, plus a $50,000 bonus for each trip, sources told the Financial Times .
That “danger money” is up from regular pay of about $15,000 a month, and is necessary for shipowners to keep their fleets crewed.
Meanwhile, sailors typically make at little as $1,500 a month. But trips through Hormuz can bump up earnings by at least four to six times their normal rates, the report said.
Other hot spots also offer hazard enhancements, albeit less than what’s available for Hormuz trips. According to the FT , captains and sailors get double pay in the southern Red Sea , where Houthis have been attacking Saudi ships, and in the Gulf of Oman, where many ship-to-ship transfers take place after Hormuz shuttle runs.
Because many ships and their crews are dedicated to the shuttle runs, they are in constant peril—allowing them to stack up all the bonuses and danger money for each trip.
A source told the FT that those brave enough to stomach the near-constant threat of attacks are “almost being viewed as mercenaries,” though some unwilling crew members are reportedly being pressured to stay onboard.
Since the Iran war started on Feb. 28, at least 93 ships have been hit, and 24 sailors have been killed, according to the International Maritime Organization.
In addition to the hazard pay for crews, shipowners are also paying for insurance, and the war risk can command 6%-10% of a ship’s value—translating to up to $20 million for a supertanker sailing through the Gulf.
All the added costs have made shipping expensive too. Freight rates for cargoes crossing the Strait of Hormuz hit a record high of $1.3 million per day, up from last year’s daily rate of $20,000-$50,000.
All the ships needed to get oil out of the Gulf have also contributed to a global tanker shortage that’s spiked freight rates around the world.
Shipbroker Gibson  pointed out that hiring a tanker to travel from the U.S. to China costs about $80 million, more than the $74 million price tag for a standard SpaceX Falcon 9 launch. Brokerage SSY estimated that rates are now the highest since the advent of the supertanker in the 1960s, even after adjusting for inflation.
Shipping costs have become so extreme that oil producers and even commodities traders are looking to own their own tankers to control the expenses.
But if freight costs get too high, they could erase the margins that can be earned from oil and refined fuels. For instance, European refiner Repsol saw its margin drop from $36 per barrel in the third quarter to $15 in October, according to analysts at RBC. Further reduction in margins could eventually force refiners to reduce how much crude they process.
The hazard premium could get worse in the Persian Gulf. Analysts have warned the Iranian regime, facing an existential threat to its rule, could re-escalate the war and take back its grip on the oil trade.
Esfandyar Batmanghelidj, founder and CEO of the Bourse & Bazaar Foundation think tank, pointed out recently that Iran can still destroy regional oil infrastructure, such as drilling and refining capacity, and can escalate if President Donald Trump rejects diplomatic off-ramps.
“Iran did not wage a scorched earth campaign—but it may yet do so if the current situation persists for too long,”  he posted on X  late last month. “That is what everyone who actually follows this region and its dynamics is worried about.”

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing has ridden the AI chip wave into the center of the global semiconductor conversation, and the current share price puts fresh focus on one thing: Are the cash flows that TSMC can realistically generate over time enough to underpin where the stock trades today?
Over the past 3 years, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing has returned about 417.0%, which puts a very large gain on the table that investors now need to weigh against the durability of its cash generation.
Record recent revenue tied to demand for advanced AI chips, plus heavy capital spending on new fabs and packaging, can reshape both the level and timing of the company’s future free cash flows.
If you'd rather focus on earnings, this one's for you. See why Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing's 29.8x P/E tells a different valuation story .
The issue now is whether the intrinsic value implied by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing’s cash flows, as estimated by a Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) approach, lines up with the price investors are paying in the market.
If you are evaluating Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing based on its cash flows and AI exposure, it may be useful to compare it with other AI infrastructure plays using 92 AI infrastructure stocks .
Does Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Look Pricey on Cash Flow?

items.summary: 3 Things to Watch When Taiwan Semiconductor (TSMC) Reports Earnings on Oct. 15  AOL.com
items.content:
All eyes will be on the bellwether of the semiconductor sector.
TSMC’s HPC numbers will reveal the AI market’s strengths and weaknesses.
Its 3nm chip production should account for a bigger slice of its revenue.
The bulls will expect it to raise its revenue guidance again.
10 stocks we like better than Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ›
TSMC (NYSE: TSM) , the world's top contract chipmaker, will post its full third-quarter earnings report on Oct. 15. It already disclosed that its revenue grew 50% year over year during the quarter, but three yet-to-be-released numbers might drive its stock higher or lower.
Most of TSMC's growth is being driven by its production of high-performance computing (HPC) chips for Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) and other fabless AI chipmakers . That segment accounted for two-thirds of its revenue in the second quarter, and its sequential growth accelerated in the first half of the year as the demand for AI chips (especially Nvidia's) outstripped its supply. That growth is consistently offsetting its slower production of other types of chips.
Therefore, investors should keep a close eye on TSMC's HPC revenue growth. Any hint of a slowdown could attract the bears, but a meaningful acceleration might drive its stock higher.
TSMC maintains its lead in the "process race" against Intel (NASDAQ: INTC) and other foundries by producing the world's smallest, densest, and most power-efficient chips.
Over the past year, the weight of its top-tier 3nm chips on its top line has increased, while the weight of its 5nm and 7nm nodes has decreased. The 3nm node includes Nvidia's newest Vera Rubin platform, which entered full production in early 2026. Investors will be expecting TSMC to generate even more revenue from the 3nm node in the second half of 2026.
Last but not least, the bulls will expect TSMC to raise its full-year revenue guidance again. Back in January, TSMC expected its revenue to grow in the mid-to-high 20% range in USD terms. But in its first-quarter report in April, it raised its outlook to more than 30% growth.
During its second-quarter report in July, it raised its guidance again to at least 40% growth. If it doesn't reiterate or raise that outlook -- which seems unlikely since its revenue rose 50% year over year in the third quarter -- its stock could pull back. That could also happen if it merely reiterates its revenue guidance but raises its capex guidance (as it did in the second quarter).
Therefore, TSMC could seemingly hit a home run on Oct. 15, but these three numbers could prevent its stock from rallying. They could also weigh down the broader semiconductor sector -- so investors holding chip stocks must keep a close eye on this earnings report.

items.title: US justice department investigates TV networks over Trump pool coverage
items.summary: The White House had blocked access for CNN, MS Now and Politico, leading them to restrict pool coverage.
items.content:
Image caption, The row over the White House pool affected live TV coverage of Trump events last month
The US justice department (DoJ) has said it is investigating several TV networks over whether they broke federal competition laws when they recently suspended pool coverage of President Donald Trump.
Last month, five networks paused their presidential coverage for several days in response to the Trump administration withdrawing the credentials of reporters from CNN, MS Now and Politico.
The justice department asked ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News to hand over communications related to the pool and said that the boycott could violate the Sherman Act, referring to a law that bars companies from engaging in monopolistic business practices.
Pool members usually share their material with the wider media.
A DoJ spokesperson said: "The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these ânews organisations have violated the antitrust laws."
Trump blocked CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House last month after accusing the organisations of writing "fiction or lies" about his team.
The White House later reinstated their access after a ruling from a judge. The three outlets had sued the Trump administration, arguing the restricted access violated their First Amendment rights.
The First Amendment forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.
The Trump administration has taken a number of legal actions against news publications in the US, including lawsuits over coverage of the president.
In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association.
The same month, the Trump administration moved to bar Associated Press (AP) reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing.

items.content:
House Republicans Move To Block Trump's Russia Diesel Deal
House Republicans Move To Block Trump's Russia Diesel Deal
Some Republican lawmakers are pushing back on President Donald Trump's diesel deal with Russia amid rising fuel prices.
WASHINGTON -- Republican Representative Brian Fitzpatrick plans to force a House vote on legislation blocking Russian oil purchases, challenging President Donald Trump's decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports as lawmakers warn the move could help finance Moscow's war against Ukraine.
Fitzpatrick (Republican-Pennsylvania), co-chair of the House Ukraine Caucus, announced on October 10 that he would introduce the Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act.
“We will be introducing bipartisan legislation to block any and all purchases of Russian oil,” Fitzpatrick wrote on X. “It will be forced to the Floor via discharge and it will pass overwhelmingly.”
Representative Don Bacon (Republican-Nebraska) has agreed to co-sponsor the bill. A Democratic sponsor had not been identified.
Trump Says Ukraine Should 'Get A New President' As Russia Kills At Least 20 In Air Strikes
A discharge petition can force a House vote without approval from the relevant committee or House leadership if it secures 218 signatures.
The effort faces time constraints: Congress is not scheduled to resume voting for several weeks, and the current congressional term ends in January. Any bill would also need Senate approval and could face White House opposition.
Fitzpatrick invoked former President Ronald Reagan's approach to confronting Moscow and reaffirmed congressional support for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whom Trump has again criticized.
“Russia illegally invaded Ukraine. Russia is squarely to blame,” Fitzpatrick wrote, adding that Congress and the American people stood behind Zelenskyy “until Ukrainian victory is achieved.”
The proposed legislation reflects concern among some Republicans that easing Russian energy restrictions could undermine pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Representative Michael McCaul (Republican-Texas), the former chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, warned that lifting sanctions could “fund the Kremlin's war machine -- emboldening more violence and destruction.”
He cited the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which Trump signed in September. The law authorizes the president, under specified conditions, to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on major purchasers of Russian energy. McCaul said it gave Trump leverage over Russia and China to help secure a negotiated end to the war.
Senator Lisa Murkowski (Republican-Alaska) urged Trump to use those authorities instead of allowing Russia to earn more from diesel exports.
Exclusive: A Russian Blueprint For A Cold, Dark Winter In Ukraine
“We can discuss Russia's return to global energy markets once the war is over, but in the meantime, we need to cut off everything fueling it,” she wrote on social media.
Democrats and former officials have also pointed to the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022, which prohibits Russian oil imports into the United States unless the president certifies that Russia has met specified conditions, including withdrawing from Ukraine, recognizing Ukrainian sovereignty and posing no threat to NATO.
The law passed the Senate 100-0 and the House 413-9 after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Former Representative Tom Malinowski, also a former top State Department official, urged Democratic leaders to use the law's expedited procedures to challenge the administration's decision.
“Under this law, House and Senate Democratic leaders can introduce a ‘Joint Resolution of Disapproval’ to prevent the purchase of Russian oil, which Congress then has to vote on in an expedited manner,” Malinowski wrote on social media.
Massive Russian Attack Kills At Least 22, Devastates Pryluky Apartment Block
“Schumer and Jeffries should do so ASAP,” he added, referring to Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries.
Whether the 2022 law applies to the latest arrangement remains a key question as the administration's temporary authorization for Russian diesel exports faces scrutiny.
Daniel Balson, advocacy director at Razom for Ukraine, told RFE/RL that Trump's decision undermined the purpose of the sanctions legislation passed weeks earlier.
“Three weeks ago, Congress passed the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act. This bill was designed to force other countries to lower their Russian energy dependence. President Trump's recent decision just increased our own,” Balson said.
He urged lawmakers to challenge the move to protect Ukraine and the credibility of congressional action. Although he had not seen Fitzpatrick's bill, Balson said pro-Ukraine advocates would pursue “any and all legislative avenues” to oppose the decision.
Senator Angus King, an independent from Maine who generally votes with Democrats, said in a statement that the agreement would offer little relief to American consumers while benefiting Russia.
Rubio Warns Russia's War Could Spill Beyond Ukraine's Borders
Citing administration figures, King said the deal covered 300,000 tons of diesel for October and 500,000 tons for November -- roughly equivalent to a day's diesel consumption in the United States.
“This so-called deal with Russia will do little for America and much for Vladimir Putin as he seeks to sustain his murderous campaign on Ukraine,” King said. He called the agreement “a fraud.”
Trump on October 10 renewed his attacks on Zelenskyy, saying Ukraine should hold an election and replace its president with a leader willing to reach an agreement with Russia.
“Well, I think he should have an election. And he could have settled this thing many times,” Trump told reporters.
Earlier, Trump had said Ukraine should “get a new leader who can make a deal.” He also demanded that Kyiv “damn well stop” attacking Russian oil refineries, which Ukraine has targeted to disrupt Moscow's war economy and fuel supplies.
Trump blamed Zelenskyy for failing to secure a settlement, a claim at odds with Kyiv’s position that any agreement must protect Ukraine’s sovereignty and with lawmakers’ calls to maintain pressure on Moscow. Trump also portrayed Putin as eager for peace and praised the release of Russian oil onto global markets.
“It surely looks bad. The president has always had a moral blindness when it comes to Putin. Propping up Russia's war economy is terrible,” Bacon told RFE/RL.
Trump Makes Deal With Putin On Diesel Exports. Ukraine Calls It A 'Gift'
Trump's remarks came hours after Russian strikes killed at least 20 people in the southeastern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhya.
Zelenskyy has said elections cannot be held under martial law and amid the security risks created by Russia's invasion. Ukrainian officials have also cited the need to ensure soldiers and displaced citizens can participate in a credible vote.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha issued a statement late on October 10 backing the Ukrainian president.
Zelenskyy "leads our nation in a time of war -- a war for independence, freedom, and dignity. He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well. He deserves support," Sybiha wrote on X.
European officials criticized the diesel agreement, warning that additional Russian energy revenue could help sustain the war.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Russian strikes had killed more than 80 Ukrainian civilians over the past two days and that Moscow had intensified hybrid attacks against EU member states and NATO allies.
“This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't,” Kallas said, adding that EU foreign ministers planned to announce a major new round of sanctions on October 12 targeting people and organizations supporting Moscow's war effort.
Germany also reaffirmed its commitment to existing sanctions and said it would work with European partners on further measures.
A spokesman for Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Berlin stood by its restrictions, while government spokesman Stefan Kornelius reiterated support for Ukraine. Economics Minister Katherina Reiche also backed the EU sanctions packages.
Germany's Fuels and Energy Trade Association said it did not expect the agreement to have a major effect on petrol-station prices.

‘It was a terrible thing’: Panama declares state of emergency as quake aftershocks rattle communities
More than 100 aftershocks as high as magnitude-5.8 recorded after two quakes toppled buildings and prompted evacuations
Panama’s government has declared a state of emergency on Saturday as the aftershocks of two powerful earthquakes that roiled the country shook communities for hours.
Officials did not attribute any deaths to Friday’s 7.7- and 6.6-magnitude earthquakes, but reported damages in all 10 of Panama’s provinces and two Indigenous territories.
The earthquakes toppled buildings near the epicentre and prompted evacuations across the Central American country. Seismologists recorded more than 100 aftershocks, including ones measuring magnitude 5.8, 5.5 and 5.2.
The earlier quake, also felt in neighbouring Colombia, was centred about 10km (6 miles) south-west of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, in the central province of Herrera, according to the US Geological Survey. It struck at a depth of 10km (6 miles).
A car sits crushed beneath debris from a collapsed building in Penonome, Panama. Photograph: Enea Lebrun/Reuters The presidential minister, Juan Carlos Orillac, announced the emergency during a news conference in the capital, Panama City. He said homes, schools, healthcare facilities, roads and hotels were among the damaged facilities.
Malitzie Rivera, the deputy director of the National Civil Protection System, said 27 people had been reported with injuries, ranging from minor to moderate.
Most of the damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera, Cocle and Los Santos.
Powerful 7.7-magnitude earthquake strikes Panama and triggers panic in capital
About 420 homes and the same number of public schools had been damaged, according to the Civil Protection agency. It also reported that seven hotels, at least 13 churches and nine bridges were affected by the earthquakes.
In La Villa de Los Santos, a colonial-era community about 64km (40 miles) north-east of the epicentre, homes and a historical Catholic church collapsed. People who spent the night on the streets were waiting for the government’s guidance on what to do next.
“We’ve been here since 1 pm yesterday; we haven’t moved,” Tony Jiménez, whose home partially collapsed, said, while sitting with relatives under a tent. “It was a terrible thing. I can tell you with absolute certainty that in my 90 years, I had never experienced anything like it. It was intense – truly intense.”
Elodia Oliva (94) rests in a park in downtown Tonosi, Panama, on Saturday. Photograph: Bienvenido Velasco/EPA Officials did not report any missing people on Saturday but said some communities remained cut off due to landslides and road damage.
That the country appeared to have avoided widespread deaths could be due to its strict building codes, especially governing the construction of skyscrapers in the capital, said Carlos Valdés, the head of the seismology department at the National Autonomous University of Mexico.
Messages of support and offers of assistance were sent from across the region shortly after the earthquakes. Mulino on Friday thanked fellow Latin American leaders for their support, saying he had spoken with the presidents of Chile, Uruguay and Guatemala, among others.
The US Department of State on Saturday said it mobilised a disaster response team to help local authorities with search and rescue expertise as well as aerial and on-the-ground assessments. The US government also pledged $5m for humanitarian assistance.
The US military’s southern command said two helicopters, supported by the state department’s drug-control bureau, had delivered 2,000 pounds (907kg) of food to people affected by the earthquakes.

Got $2,000? 2 Natural Gas Pipeline Stocks to Buy Before Winter.
The rapid growth of the cloud and AI markets is driving natural gas prices higher, since U.S. data centers get over 40% of their electricity from natural gas. That's been a boon for natural gas producers and the midstream pipeline companies that transport the gas.
But as winter approaches, natural gas prices will likely climb even higher as temperatures drop and heating costs rise. To profit from that shift, investors should consider investing $2,000 (or more) in these two top pipeline stocks: Energy Transfer (TXSE: ET) and The Williams Companies (NYSE: WMB).

Energy Transfer operates more than 140,000 miles of pipeline across 44 states. It transports crude oil, natural gas, natural gas liquids (NGL), and other refined products through its pipelines, and exports natural gas (LNG) through its marine export terminals.
Roughly 30% of all natural gas produced in the U.S. flows through Energy Transfer's pipelines. It typically generates around 40% of its adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) from its natural gas assets. That percentage will increase after it closes its $2.6 billion acquisition of Vaquero Midstream later this year.
Energy Transfer is a master limited partnership (MLP), which combines its own income with a return of capital to pay more tax-efficient distributions than regular corporations. That's why it pays a high forward yield of 6.6%. Those payments only consumed about half of its distributable cash flow (DCF) over the past few years, so it has plenty of room to raise its payout.
However, investors in MLPs must file an extra K-1 form to report that income every year. If you don't mind that extra work, it still looks like a bargain at 12 times this year's earnings per unit.
The Williams Companies operates over 32,000 miles of pipeline in 24 states. It's smaller than Energy Transfer, but it mainly transports natural gas and NGLs. It owns Transco, the largest natural gas pipeline in the U.S, which connects the Gulf Coast to the Atlantic Seaboard.
Williams transports about a third of all natural gas produced in the U.S., making it a more focused "pure play" on natural gas than Energy Transfer and many of its industry peers. Williams is also structured as a regular C-corporation rather than an MLP, which might make it more appealing to investors who don't want to deal with the extra tax paperwork.
Williams pays a forward dividend yield of 2.9%, which may seem low relative to other pipeline stocks, but its trailing payout ratio of 82% leaves plenty of room for future hikes. It isn't a screaming bargain at 27 times forward earnings, but its direct exposure to the booming natural gas market -- without the noise of crude oil -- could justify that higher valuation.

items.title: SCOTUS weighs local governments’ climate change lawsuits against oil, gas companies - The North State Journal
items.summary: SCOTUS weighs local governments’ climate change lawsuits against oil, gas companies  The North State Journal
items.content:
Climate activists gather outside the Supreme Court as the nation’s high court hears arguments in Suncor Energy v. Boulder County on Monday in Washington, D.C. (Manuel Balce Ceneta / AP
WASHINGTON, D.C. — The Supreme Court grappled Monday with whether local governments can sue oil and gas companies in state court to help cover costs associated with climate change, an issue with potentially billions of dollars at stake.
Key justices appeared wary about the potential sweep of litigation but torn over the complex questions of federal and state law raised by the case.
Officials in Boulder argue their lawsuit is an attempt to hold energy companies Suncor and ExxonMobil accountable for their contributions to climate change.
They say that worsening disasters such as floods and wildfires put a heavy financial burden on local communities, and the industry should bear part of that cost.
The city and county of Boulder first sued the oil companies in 2018, years before the 2021 Marshall Fire destroyed nearly 1,100 homes and left two people dead. Total damage was estimated at $2 billion, making it the costliest wildfire in Colorado history.
Boulder case part of wave of legal action against oil companies
Governments from largely blue-leaning areas around the country have filed similar lawsuits seeking damages that could total billions of dollars, part of a wave of legal action worldwide seeking to leverage action through the courts.
“Presumably, if you prevail, the next day, a municipality in every single state will file a lawsuit,” said Chief Justice John Roberts. “How do you think that will work out on the ground?”
Justice Brett Kavanaugh said a win by Boulder could bankrupt the oil companies and other potential defendants.
“I mean, anyone is a potential defendant for a suit like this. Any manufacturer, any business,” he said.
A win for the oil and gas companies at the Supreme Court, meanwhile, could shut down dozens of similar cases filed in recent years.
Suncor and Exxon argue that the Clean Air Act gives the federal government — not the states — the power to regulate emissions.
They have the support of the Trump administration, which argues the lawsuits are an unconstitutional attempt to regulate planet-warming emissions and impose Colorado’s state law beyond its borders.
But Roberts and other justices pointed out that state courts consider lawsuits about myriad issues that have nationwide reach.
“I guess I’m not quite sure what makes this situation different from those,” Roberts said.
The court is also weighing a jurisdictional question that could allow it an “off-ramp” to avoid deciding the issues right away. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson seemed like a vote in favor of that path.
“Why shouldn’t we wait and hear all of these claims once the state courts are done?” she asked.
The case was heard without Justice Samuel Alito, who recused himself just a week before arguments after facing calls to step aside because he owns stock in oil companies. That raises the possibility of a tie vote.
A deadlock would leave in place a decision from Colorado’s highest court allowing the case to proceed.
Attorney Kannon Shanmugam, representing the industry, urged the justices to reverse that ruling. He said the Boulder case was attempting to use the courts to decide a public policy issue that is properly up to Congress and other elected officials.
“Climate change is certainly one of the most pressing issues” facing the country, but the lawsuit “is exactly the wrong way to go about” addressing it, he said.
Principal Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris said Boulder’s case “egregiously exceeds” the state’s authority. The county essentially declares itself a victim of actions that occurred largely out of state, she said.
But Kevin Russell, an attorney representing Boulder, argued that state lawsuits can address damage in Colorado, regardless of where the fossil fuels are produced.
Boulder is not trying to regulate greenhouse gas emissions or stop the companies from continuing to produce oil and gas, Russell said. Instead, officials are seeking to hold the companies accountable for allegedly misleading the public about their contribution to global warming by burning fossil fuels, he said.
“Chapter 3” of case trilogy, after tobacco and opioids
Justice Elena Kagan compared the climate case to previous state-based lawsuits against the tobacco industry and opioid makers.
“This is Chapter 3,” she said, noting the similarities of states claiming harms from products produced nationally and even internationally.
“This is a different book,” replied Shanmugam, the industry lawyer. Harms claimed by Boulder “are diffused nationwide and indeed worldwide,” he said.
Trump’s Republican administration has rolled back environmental regulations, including a move last month by the Environmental Protection Agency to repeal rules that limit emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas. States and cities have already sued over the repeal of the power plant rule.

Germany to Release Up to 15 mmbbl of Oil Under G7 Plan | Egypt Oil & Gas
Germany to Release Up to 15 mmbbl of Oil Under G7 Plan
Germany will release up to 15 million barrels (mmbbl) of crude oil and petroleum products from its emergency reserves under a coordinated Group of Seven (G7) initiative led by the International Energy Agency (IEA), Reuters reported.  The move aims to ease fuel shortages and contain rising energy prices amid supply disruptions linked to conflicts involving Iran and Ukraine.
The Group of Seven (G7) is an intergovernmental coalition formed by Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the UK, the US, and the EU.
The planned release includes diesel and heating oil, alongside crude oil, making Germany a major contributor to efforts to improve the availability of refined petroleum products. The initiative reflects growing concern over diesel supplies, which are critical to transportation, agriculture, and industrial activity.
Under the G7's October 2 agreement , member countries committed to coordinate the IEA's release of 100 million barrels of oil over four months, with a substantial portion of the diesel release scheduled to begin within the first 20 days. The group also called for coordination of refinery maintenance and higher refinery utilization where feasible to increase fuel availability
The IEA announced on March 11, 2026, that its 32 member countries would make 400 million barrels of oil available from emergency reserves in response to disruptions caused by the Middle East conflict. The agency said oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz had fallen to less than 10% of pre-conflict levels, highlighting the scale of the supply shock.

Vaalco Reports Positive Gabon Well Results, Advances Côte d’Ivoire Drilling | Egypt Oil & Gas
Vaalco Reports Positive Gabon Well Results, Advances Côte d’Ivoire Drilling
Vaalco Energy, a US-based independent energy company, has completed the third phase of its offshore drilling campaign in Gabon, reporting positive results from the ETSEM-3H well in the Southeast Etame field.
Vaalco achieved a stabilized initial production rate of around 2,000 barrels of oil per day (bbl/d) gross, including 1,140 bbl/d net to the company, according to a press release by the company.
The well was drilled with a 300-meter lateral wellbore and encountered net pay in high-quality Gamba reservoir sands.
“This represents the final well in our successful Phase 3 drilling campaign, and the drilling rig has now been demobilized from the field,” said George Maxwell, CEO of Vaalco Energy.
Separately, the company has started the fifth phase of its drilling campaign at the Baobab field offshore Côte d’Ivoire, with the production expected to come online near the end of 2026.
“Following the successful restart of the Baobab field during the second quarter, we have now commenced the Phase 5 drilling campaign with batch-setting the top-hole sections of the new wells,” Maxwell said.
The campaign is planned to include four production wells, three water injectors and two workovers. Vaalco expects the new wells to deliver meaningful production increases in 2027, according to Maxwell.
Vaalco has a diversified portfolio of production, development and exploration assets in Gabon, Egypt, Côte d’Ivoire and Equatorial Guinea.

items.title: DIU publishes data on 20 Russian shadow fleet vessels carrying oil and gas - Ukrinform
items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.
items.content:
Ukraine's defense intelligence has published data on 20 vessels involved in exporting Russian crude oil, petroleum products and liquefied natural gas, as well as bunkering sanctioned vessels.
The Defense Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) reported this on Telegram , according to Ukrinform.
"These vessels are part of the logistics network that the Kremlin uses to generate revenue to finance its genocidal war against Ukraine. All of them are currently under sanctions imposed by the United Kingdom or Ukraine, while one of the vessels is subject to U.S. restrictions," the statement said.
The DIU highlighted Russian vessel PORTOVYY (IMO 9246621) among the main subjects of the publication. The vessel is designed to transport and store liquefied natural gas (LNG).
The agency said that since 2021, the tanker has been owned by sanctioned Russian company PJSC Gazprom and has served as a floating gas storage facility at the Portovaya complex in the Leningrad region.
"On August 15, 2026, PORTOVYY, carrying a cargo of Russian LNG, left the Gulf of Finland for the first time since November 2021. The tanker sailed along the Northern Sea Route to the Chinese port of Beihai for unloading," the agency said.
The vessel is currently at the Zhoushan Huafeng Shipyard on Zhoushan Island in China, which has been designated as the site for its maintenance.
The agency also published details about two new vessels involved in Russia's shadow fleet of gas carriers, which the aggressor state hastily acquired through front companies around the world in spring 2026.
They are the conventional LNG tanker AVACHA (IMO 9319404) and the gas carrier CHAIVO (IMO 9319404).
AVACHA was previously owned by China's Jovo Energy but was acquired in spring 2026 by the little-known company Tudor Maritime Ltd, registered in the Marshall Islands.
Since June 2026, the conventional LNG tanker has sailed under the Russian flag and has been operated by the newly established Russian entity Kryoline Management LLC (TIN 6500028647).
According to the agency, since August 2026 the vessel has been transporting gas from the Utrenny terminal of the sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 project to the Beihai hub in China.
CHAIVO was previously owned by Greece's Maran Gas Maritime but was also acquired by Tudor Maritime Ltd.
"Since July 2026, the vessel has been transferred to the Russian flag and placed under the umbrella of Kryoline Management LLC. Since August this year, the gas carrier has been transporting cargoes to the port of Beihai from the sanctioned non-self-propelled floating gas storage unit KORYAK FSU, located in the waters of the port of Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky," the DIU said.
The agency explained that, in an effort to preserve critically important revenues from energy exports, Russia is not only attempting to build ice-class vessels at its own shipyards but is also systematically and proactively expanding its shadow fleet through a network of offshore companies.
Read also: UK imposes new sanctions on Russia's oil, shadow fleet , war supply chains
The agency called on foreign partners to coordinate their efforts, including by strengthening controls over the sale of vessels owned by commercial entities, decisively cutting off Russia's energy revenues that are converted into weapons used against civilians, and blocking opportunities for sanctioned vessels to receive services at foreign shipyards.
"Every Russian tanker carrying sanctioned oil or gas is a legitimate target for international sanctions pressure," the agency said.
As reported, the DIU uncovered a scheme used by Russian agricultural tycoons to evade sanctions while generating revenue in the EU to finance the war against Ukraine.
